quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
  archived         a verbatim copy stored in POSITIONS-history.md by a later commit
  re-created       a text new in POSITIONS.md made from an earlier text (archived or removed)
  restored         a text back in POSITIONS.md verbatim from POSITIONS-history.md
  renumbered       the same text under a new number (2026-10-13: none -> P-n)
  struck           the number left POSITIONS.md (the first event of a struck entry's trail)
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
it precedes, and its first 300 characters; then how many candidates there were in all.

**`label` is not a goto.** It's a named block that code inside it can leave early, with a value. Rust's labelled `break` with a value and Scala's `boundary`/`break` are the nearest equivalents.

```
label search
  ...
  exit search with x   (leaves the block; the block's value is x)
  ...
end search
```

`exit` can only jump to the end of a `label` that encloses it, never anywhere else. If no `exit` runs, the block's value is its last expression.

**The expected type.** Yes, Fortress works like Scala and Swift here: a block's value is its last expression, and a function's body is that expression.
- The checker carries "the type this spot needs" down into an expression. A function body gets its declared return type, and the block passes it on to its last expression.
- This matters for one kind of function. In `fail[\T\](s: String): T`, `T` appears only in the result, so the arguments can't fix it. Only the expected type can.
- Example: in `x: ZZ32 = fail("bad")`, `T` becomes `ZZ32`.
- Where nothing is expected, `T` falls back to its bound, `Any`.

**`typecase`, and what batch 11's Q2 decided.**
- `typecase v of A => e1; B => e2 end` picks a branch by `v`'s run-time type.
- Its type is the union of its branches' types, so each branch gets the type the whole `typecase` is expected to have.
- Q2 asked whether a call inside a branch gets that expected type. The batch made it so.
- You're right that we didn't go through it in detail. You accepted Q1 to Q4 at their recommendations in one answer on 10-08, around 21:40 UTC, along with the other decisions of that evening.

**`label`, Q48(a).** It's the same idea with an early exit added: the block's type is the union of its last expression and its `exit` values. The real case is `String.fss:431`:

```

    ...checks...
    typecase baseString of
        s:CatString => do ... end
        EmptyString => fail "SubString of EmptyString"
        SubString   => fail "SubString of SubString"

end methodVerify
```

`verify` is declared to return `()`. The checker passes `()` into the `typecase` branches, as batch 11 made it do, but not into a `label` body. So `fail`'s `T` becomes `Any`, and the method is refused. With (a), the `label` body gets `()`, the same as any function body would.

    The compiled checker retries a call written as another call's argument against each declaration's parameter type

The coercions that the instance needs are inserted into the call statically,
as is any coercion that \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses.

\emph{The expected type.}
A call has an expected type in these contexts: as the right-hand side of a
variable or field declaration that declares its type, that type; as the
right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, that
type; as the body of a functional that declares its return type, that type;
as the last expression of a block that has an expected type, whether or not
local declarations precede it in the block, the block's expected type; as a
branch of an \KWD{if} expression with an \KWD{else} clause that has an
expected type, the expected type of the \KWD{if} expression; as a clause of an
\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, \TYP{()}, the type that
every such clause must have (\secref{if-expr}); as a clause of a
\KWD{typecase} expression that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause
among them, the expected type of the \KWD{typecase} expression, of which the
union of the types of its clauses, the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression
(\secref{typecase}), is then a subtype where the type of each clause is;
as the body of a \KWD{label} expression that has an expected type, or as the
\KWD{with} clause expression of an \KWD{exit} expression whose target is that
\KWD{label} expression, the expected type of the \KWD{label} expression, of
which the union of the type of its body and the types of those \KWD{with}
clause values, the type of the \KWD{label} expression (\secref{label-expr}),
is then a subtype where each of those types is; and as an argument of a call
that this section does not accept with its arguments typed without an expected
type, where the argument is itself a call with inferred static arguments, the
parameter type at the argument's position of each declaration
of the enclosing call in turn, instantiated, where that declaration has static
parameters, by the arguments that are not so typed and by the expected type of
the enclosing call alone, as described below.
The expected type is used whether the call is written by tight juxtaposition,
as \EXP{f(x)} (\secref{juxtameaning}), or by loose juxtaposition, as
\EXP{f\;x}, or as a method invocation or an operator application.

gave the last expression of a block an expected type only where no local
declaration precedes it, and gave none to a clause of an \KWD{if} expression

14:4. **My 22 probe calls.** Stock accepts 3. Wide accepts 18, narrow 13. Every call accepted compiled and ran with the instance shown in section 2, except a varargs callee: it checks, but code generation has no varargs ("Can't compile VarArgs yet"), whatever the retry. Four calls stay refused under both, rightly: three ill-typed controls and one true ambiguity.
15:5. **The compiler track** (`ant testCompiler`: compiler 1,078 tests, othercompiler 263). Two verdicts change under wide, both expected failures whose defect the retry repairs: `XXXInferContextDrops` (row 455) and `XXXInferLoneUnionClosedTrait` (row 535's pinned refusal, which now compiles and runs with `T = Fig`). 22:## 1. What I built
24:### The mechanism
30:- It picks the arguments that are calls carrying static arguments (wide), or calls one of whose declarations has a type parameter its parameter types do not mention (narrow).
38:### The patch (wide), against fe74fb738

207:## 2. The faces and my programs [measured]
209:`BoxT[\T\](v: ZZ32)` is an object whose `T` only its type mentions. `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`, `wrapT[\T\](x: T): BoxT[\T\]`, `idB[\T\](b: BoxT[\T\]): BoxT[\T\]`. Under the compiled path an unbounded `T` has the bound `Object`. Each line: stock / wide / narrow, then the instance the run printed (a `typecase` on the box, so the instance is the run time's own). All 22 calls are in one checked program. The accepted ones are in a run program: wide's compiled and run at 1 and 4 threads, narrow's at 1.

273:Under wide:
279:Under narrow, the same, with the argument limited to "a call of a declaration with a type parameter that only its return type mentions". The item at `:266-268` then keeps "any other argument of another call", which `takesBox64(wrapT(3))` is.

285:1. **Wide or narrow.** Wide clears both faces and row 535's shape; narrow clears one face. Neither moves the distance or a passing test. Wide is the same rule every other context already follows: try without the expected type, keep it if it fits, else with it.
286:2. **A generic outer callee fixed only by retried arguments.** `pair(mk(), wrapT(3))`: wide instantiates `pair` from the other arguments and the context only, so with both arguments retried `U` takes its bound, `Object`. 61: narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's parameter types (item 51).** It is the team's rule of 2012, in Steele's compiled checker and Welterweigh
- P-49 **The checker tries a call without the expected type first, and with coercion only after (row 508).** It keeps the first attempt, by subtyping, when its result converts to the expected type, and only then tries coercion with the context. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one reached by coercion.
- P-50 **A `label` body takes the expected type of the whole `label` (item 48 (a)).** The specification types a `label` as the union of its body's last expression and its exits' `with` values. So the checker passes the expected type of the whole into the body and into the exits' values, as for a `typecase` clause, and the inference chapter lists both contexts. P-51 is the other half of item 48. Row 642 stays `CONTESTED` only because the ledger's tool cannot close it.
- P-51 **A call written as another call's argument is retried against each declaration's parameter type (item 48 (b), row 455).** When the checker's attempts at a call keep none, an argument that is a call with inferred static arguments is checked again, with each candidate's parameter type as its expected type. The trigger is wide: any inferred static argument, not only a result-only type parameter. Why: it makes the inference rules one rule everywhere, past the cases the team built. Its probe moves no error of the distance. Its rung promotes the expected failures `XXXInferContextDrops` and `XXXInferLoneUnionClosedTrait`, whose refusals it repairs. Built by climb batch 14 (`0856f3e6a`).
- P-52 **A range of rank 2 or 3 checks containment corner by corner (item 50, row 657).** The bounds check behind `narrowToRange` compares the other range's bounds by the ranges' point-by-point order, `PCMP`, not by the tuple order, which serves sorting. So `((0,0):(9,9)).narrowToRange((2,-1):(5,5))` raises `IndexOutOfBounds`.
